Kiko the Kangaroo

Kiko the Kangaroo is a fictional kangaroo appearing in theatrical cartoons produced by Terrytoons. He is featured in ten cartoons made between 1936 and 1937.

As with various anthropomorphic animals at the time, Kiko wears shorts and shoes. While he does not speak, the marsupial is skilled in hand-to-hand fighting, and would use his prowess to defend his troubled friends or subdue an opponent in a boxing match. He can also use his tail for various purposes. Kiko was created by Terrytoons in a desperate attempt to rival characters of other studios. He first appeared in Farmer Al Falfa's Prize Package as a pet sent to the farmer by the latter's brother. Since then, the kangaroo would spend the rest of his short theatrical run in a series of his own. After only ten cartoons were released, plans were made to create another cartoon featuring him, only to be not approved by Paul Terry. Kiko is also among the few characters of the studio to have a theme song. He also has merchandise including plush toys.

Below is a list of films in their original titles. Some of them later came with alternate names when distributed by other companies like Castle Films.

seminar announcement

The Department of Urban Planning at State University is pleased to announce the upcoming "Future Cities 2024" seminar, scheduled for Saturday, October 12, from 9:00 AM to 4:00 PM in the Grand Hall of the Main Library. This event is designed to bring together city planners, architects, environmental scientists, and community leaders to discuss the pivotal role of sustainable design in the development of modern metropolitan areas. The primary objective of this gathering is to provide a platform for the exchange of innovative strategies that can help mitigate climate change impacts while enhancing the quality of life for urban residents. Attendees will have the opportunity to engage in detailed discussions with leading experts in the field who have successfully implemented green infrastructure projects in various international cities.

The seminar will feature a series of keynotes followed by interactive panel discussions. The opening keynote is delivered by Dr. Elena Rossi, a renowned sustainability architect, who will present her latest research on biophilic design principles and their application in high-density housing projects. Following her address, a panel of four experts will debate the economic viability of comprehensive urban greenery initiatives. This segment is particularly relevant for policy makers who are currently drafting new zoning laws for the fiscal year. The afternoon session will include two breakout workshops focused on water management systems and pedestrian-friendly street design. Participants are encouraged to bring specific case studies from their own regions to facilitate more targeted peer-to-peer learning during these small group activities.

Registration for the event is open to all professionals, students, and community members interested in urban development. The general admission fee is fifty dollars, which includes lunch and access to all keynote presentations and panel discussions. Students and early career professionals can register for a reduced fee of twenty-five dollars by presenting a valid ID upon check-in. A limited number of complimentary tickets are available for non-profit organizations working directly on local neighborhood revitalization projects. To secure your spot, please visit the university's events portal and complete the online registration form by October 1st. Late registrations may be subject to additional processing fees depending on capacity constraints.

The venue is located in the heart of the city center, easily accessible via public transit lines 4 and 9. Free parking is available in the visitor lot adjacent to the library for those who prefer to drive. The venue is fully wheelchair accessible, and real-time captioning services will be provided for all keynote speeches to ensure inclusivity for all attendees. For those requiring dietary accommodations, there will be a variety of options available during the lunch break, including vegetarian, vegan, and gluten-free meals. Please indicate any specific dietary requirements during the registration process so that the catering team can ensure a comfortable experience for every guest.

Preparation for the seminar is minimal but recommended. Attendees are advised to review the attached agenda and speaker bios before the event to maximize the value of their participation. Networking opportunities will be integrated throughout the day, with a dedicated reception space available for informal conversations between sessions. The final panel discussion will address emerging technologies in smart city infrastructure, providing a forward-looking perspective on how data analytics can support sustainable urban growth. We encourage all participants to arrive early to enjoy the morning coffee and pastries while meeting fellow attendees. This event represents a significant step toward fostering a collaborative approach to planning the cities of tomorrow, and we look forward to welcoming you to what promises to be an intellectually stimulating day.

This memorandum outlines the current home internet service tiers available for employee recommendation and customer inquiry handling. The primary focus is on the Essential, Standard, and Premium packages, each tailored to different bandwidth needs and household sizes.

The Essential package offers speeds up to 250 Mbps, suitable for single users or small households engaged in basic web browsing, email, and standard definition video streaming. The Standard plan increases capability with symmetric speeds of 600 Mbps, designed for medium-sized households where multiple devices operate simultaneously. It supports high definition streaming across four or more TVs, online gaming with low latency, and regular video conferencing for remote work scenarios without significant performance degradation.

For power users and large families, the Premium tier delivers 1.2 Gbps download and 600 Mbps upload speeds. This configuration handles multiple 4K streams, frequent large file transfers, and professional creative workflows such as video editing. It also includes enhanced security features and priority traffic routing during peak network congestion periods.

All plans include a Wi-Fi 6 router and installation service at no additional cost. Monthly fees are fixed for the first twelve months, after which rates may adjust according to the standard annual price review policy. Customers may upgrade or downgrade their service at any time, subject to a thirty-day processing period for hardware swaps or line changes.

volcano science

Volcano science has moved from the realm of myth and disaster into a precise, data-driven discipline that helps protect lives and property. Modern researchers combine satellite imagery, seismic networks, and gas measurements to create a continuous picture of what lies beneath a volcano's surface. By tracking subtle ground deformation with GPS and InSAR, scientists can detect the slow swelling of magma chambers weeks or even months before an eruption, giving authorities a critical window to prepare evacuation plans and mitigate risk.

At the heart of volcanic activity is the behavior of molten rock, or magma, as it travels through the Earth's crust. Recent advances in petrology and high-temperature experiments have revealed how crystal content, volatile gases, and temperature control magma's viscosity, which in turn dictates the explosiveness of an eruption. Low-viscosity basaltic magma can flow freely, forming shield volcanoes and extensive lava fields, whereas silica-rich magmas become highly viscous, trapping gases that eventually explode with devastating force. Understanding these internal properties helps forecasters predict the style of an upcoming eruption.

Monitoring volcanic gases, especially sulfur dioxide and carbon dioxide, offers another vital clue. Remote sensing instruments on aircraft and satellites can measure gas plumes with remarkable precision, while ground-based spectrometers provide real-time data on emissions. A sudden surge in sulfur dioxide often signals that fresh magma has reached shallow depths, a precursor to potential explosive activity. Coupled with seismic tremor patterns, gas data form a multi-parameter approach that reduces uncertainty and improves warning times for nearby communities.

The social dimension of volcano science is equally important. Researchers collaborate with emergency managers, local governments, and indigenous groups to translate technical findings into actionable plans. Public education campaigns, community drills, and transparent communication of risk levels foster trust and ensure that warnings are heeded when they matter most. In places like Hawaii, Italy, and Indonesia, such partnerships have saved countless lives by turning scientific insight into practical preparedness.

Looking ahead, the integration of artificial intelligence and machine learning promises to refine eruption forecasts even further. By feeding decades of seismic, deformation, and gas data into sophisticated algorithms, scientists can identify patterns that elude human analysts. Early prototypes already demonstrate the ability to flag anomalous activity with higher confidence, opening the door to automated alerts that could shave precious hours off response times. As these tools mature, volcano science will continue to evolve from observation to prediction, offering a clearer safeguard against one of Earth's most powerful natural forces.

Navigating the recommended immunization timeline can often feel overwhelming for new parents and long-time healthcare seekers alike. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention maintains a comprehensive schedule designed to protect individuals from childhood through adulthood. This roadmap is not static but evolves based on scientific research and public health data. Understanding the baseline sequence helps families prepare for well-child visits and ensures that no critical protection is overlooked. The goal is to build robust immunity at the most effective age windows for each specific pathogen.

Infancy marks the most intensive phase of the vaccination journey. From the very first moments of life, newborns receive the Hepatitis B shot, followed by a rapid series of doses for diseases like diphtheria, tetanus, pertussis, and polio during the second, fourth, and six-month checkups. Rotavirus and pneumococcal vaccines are also introduced during this early window to guard against common but potentially severe gastrointestinal and respiratory infections. Pediatricians emphasize the importance of keeping up with these monthly or bi-monthly appointments to minimize the risk of exposure in crowded daycare settings.

As children approach kindergarten age, the focus shifts to reinforcing existing protections and adding new ones. Boosters for the earlier administered vaccines are given to maintain immunity levels. At this stage, measles, mumps, and rubella vaccines are administered to prevent outbreaks that can spread rapidly in school environments. Varicella, or chickenpox, is also targeted during these years. These shots are crucial because they serve as a final layer of defense before a child enters more complex social structures where disease transmission rates increase significantly.

Puberty and early adulthood introduce additional considerations, particularly for adolescents. Human Papillomavirus vaccines become a priority to prevent certain cancers and genital warts, with recommendations now extending slightly later than traditional teen years in some guidelines. Meningococcal vaccines are often started around age eleven to protect against meningitis, which can be particularly dangerous for teenagers and college students living in dormitories. These vaccines address specific risks associated with adolescent lifestyle changes and emerging social environments.

Beyond childhood, adult health maintenance continues with periodic boosters and new recommendations. Shingles vaccinations are advised for older adults to prevent a painful reactivation of the chickenpox virus, while annual flu shots remain a staple for all age groups. Tetanus and diphtheria boosters are recommended every ten years throughout one's life. It is essential for adults to discuss personal medical history, travel plans, and occupation with their healthcare providers to tailor this general schedule to individual needs, ensuring comprehensive and lifelong protection.

Richard Tobin obtained a Bachelor of Arts degree from Norwich University (Northfield, Vermont) and received a Master of Business Administration from Drexel University (Philadelphia). Prior to beginning his business career, Tobin served as an Officer in the United States Army from 1985 to 1989.

Furthermore, Richard Tobin holds the position of Vice Chairman of Turk Traktor ve Ziraat Makineleri AS of Ankara (Turkey), and serves on the Board of Directors for the Dover Corporation of Downers Grove, Illinois. He sits on the U.S. Chamber of Commerce Board of Directors, and is a member of the Business Roundtable. On December 10, 2021, the KeyCorp Board of Directors elected Richard J. Tobin to the Board of Directors.

airline baggage rules

Navigating airline baggage rules can often feel like deciphering a secret code. What seems straightforward on the surface quickly reveals layers of complexity, varying wildly from one carrier to the next, and even between different fare types on the same airline. Understanding these nuances before you head to the airport is not just about avoiding unexpected fees; it's about ensuring a smooth, stress-free start to your journey.

For carry-on luggage, the golden rule is consistency in inconsistency. While most airlines adhere to a general guideline for dimensions, typically allowing a bag that fits in the overhead bin, the specific measurements can differ by a few inches, making a significant impact. Weight restrictions for carry-ons are also increasingly common, especially with budget airlines. Remember the TSA's 3-1-1 rule for liquids in your carry-on: containers must be 3.4 ounces (100 milliliters) or smaller, fit in a 1-quart-sized bag, and be limited to one bag per passenger.

Checked baggage presents another set of variables. The number of complimentary bags, if any, often depends on your fare class, frequent flyer status, or the route you're flying. Economy class often means paying for the first checked bag, while premium cabins or certain credit card holders might enjoy one or two free. Crucially, pay close attention to weight limits, usually 50 pounds (23 kg) for most economy tickets. Exceeding this will almost certainly trigger hefty overweight baggage fees.

Beyond standard suitcases, special items like sports equipment, musical instruments, or oversized items have their own distinct rules and often require advance notification. Policies for these can be particularly intricate, involving specific packaging requirements, additional fees, and sometimes even requiring them to be shipped as cargo. Always consult your airline's website directly for comprehensive details on these less common items.

The best strategy for mastering baggage rules is proactive research. Before you even start packing, visit your airline's official website and locate their baggage policy page. Enter your specific flight details, including your destination and fare class, to get the most accurate and up-to-date information. Many airlines also offer a baggage calculator tool, which can be incredibly helpful.

Consider investing in a small luggage scale to weigh your bags at home, preventing any unwelcome surprises at the check-in counter. If you travel frequently, look into airline-branded credit cards or loyalty programs, as many offer benefits like a free first checked bag. A little preparation goes a long way in saving both money and peace of mind when flying.

budget laptops

The market for budget laptops has undergone a significant transformation over the last few years, shifting from a landscape of compromise to one of genuine value. For many consumers, a laptop under five hundred dollars is no longer a stopgap solution but a capable primary device for daily tasks. Modern processors, even in the entry-level range, offer sufficient power for web browsing, streaming high-definition video, and handling document-based work with remarkable ease. This evolution means that students, remote workers, and casual users can now purchase reliable hardware without depleting their savings, making technology more accessible than ever before.

When shopping for an affordable machine, the screen quality is often the first area where manufacturers cut costs, but it should not be ignored. A bright, high-resolution panel can make the difference between eye strain and comfort during long usage sessions. While you likely will not find the premium color accuracy of a high-end creator tool, looking for displays that meet basic brightness standards ensures usability in well-lit environments. Additionally, keying out for models with anti-glare finishes can significantly improve the experience, reducing reflections from windows and overhead lights that frequently plague lower-tier hardware.

Connectivity and port selection are critical features that often go overlooked until after the purchase. Many ultra-thin budget laptops rely heavily on USB-C for power and data, which is convenient for travel but problematic if you still use USB-A devices or standard HDMI ports. Before finalizing a choice, consider your daily peripherals. If you frequently plug in older flash drives or project onto a monitor, prioritize a model that retains at least one USB-A port or comes with a multi-port dongle in the box. This small detail prevents the immediate need for additional adapters.

Battery life is another essential metric that defines the true portability of a budget device. While specification sheets often list theoretical maximums, real-world performance varies based on screen brightness and background applications. Aim for models that promise at least eight hours of battery life, as this ensures the laptop can last through a full workday or lecture schedule without hunting for a power outlet. Lithium-polymer batteries are standard in this price range, offering a good balance between energy density and weight, allowing you to carry the device easily between locations.

Finally, reliability and warranty terms should play a substantial role in the decision-making process. A cheap laptop is only a good deal if it continues to function for several years without requiring frequent repairs. Look for brands that offer at least a one-year limited warranty and accessible customer support options. Reading verified user reviews can provide insights into long-term durability, highlighting common failure points such as hinge wear or keyboard responsiveness. By focusing on these fundamental aspects rather than flashy marketing features, you can secure a dependable tool that serves your needs efficiently for years to come.

Trevor's World of Sport

Trevor's World of Sport began as a 2003 BBC television sitcom written and directed by Andy Hamilton and starring Neil Pearson as Trevor. One series of the television series was made, followed by three series which were aired on BBC Radio 4, as a continuation of the television series.

Neil Pearson as Trevor Heslop Paul Reynolds as Sammy Dobbs Rosalind Ayres as Theresa Abdul Salis as Barry Cosima Shaw as Heidrun Michael Fenton Stevens as Ralph Renton Claire Skinner as Meryl

The series is set in the world of TS Sports - a sports public relations firm, run by Trevor Heslop and his partner, the lascivious Sammy Dobbs (Paul Reynolds). Trevor is portrayed as an essentially decent, honest man in the corrupt money-obsessed industry of sporting celebrity, who is still deeply in love with his estranged wife Meryl (Claire Skinner). The other TS Sports office staff are the cool German receptionist Heidrun (Cosima Shaw), whose lesbianism obsesses Sammy; the young black trainee Barry (Abdul Salis); and strongly Christian office manager Theresa (Rosalind Ayres). Andy Hamilton also appears in a minor role within the show, and several actors who have worked in his other comedy shows for television and radio appear. Neil Pearson was in Hamilton's Drop the Dead Donkey, as (briefly) was Michael Fenton Stevens who plays TS Sports' only regular client, fading celebrity Ralph Renton.

Only one television series was made, and Hamilton felt mistreated by the BBC over the scheduling of the show. The first episode attracted an average of 3.4 million viewers, dropping to 2.9 million for the second and third episodes. The subsequent episodes were rescheduled from Friday evenings (just after the 9:00pm watershed) to Monday nights (after the 10:00pm news), despite the Radio Times issues having already been published listing the originally scheduled transmission dates. Hamilton went public with his displeasure over the show's scheduling and vowed never to work for BBC1 again, though he has since changed his mind. A radio version was first broadcast on BBC Radio 4 in 2004, with subsequent series in 2005 and 2007.

ocean tides

Each morning, coastal residents walk the shoreline to mark how far the water has receded. These daily rhythms are not random but follow a precise pattern driven by the moon's gravitational pull. While the sun also exerts influence, its effect is roughly half that of the moon because of its greater distance from Earth. Understanding these shifts is crucial for anyone living near the sea.

High tide occurs when the ocean bulges toward the moon, or in the case of spring tides, when both celestial bodies align. At this peak, waves wash further up the beach, submerging rocks that are usually exposed. Conversely, low tide reveals vast stretches of sand and mud. Between these extremes lies the intermediate state where many marine creatures become accessible to foragers and curious observers.

The cycle doubles the visual appeal of the shoreline. At low tide, tide pools form in crevices, creating temporary ecosystems teeming with starfish, crabs, and algae. These micro habitats are fragile and sensitive to temperature and sunlight. Observers are encouraged to look but not touch, respecting the delicate balance that allows life to thrive in these narrow margins between land and deep water.

However, tides are not merely a scenic backdrop; they are a powerful force. Undercurrents known as rip currents can form suddenly during the transition from high to low tide. These fast-moving channels of water pull swimmers offshore with terrifying speed. Local authorities often post warnings and close beaches when conditions become hazardous. Ignoring these signs can lead to dangerous situations for even experienced swimmers.

For coastal communities, accurate tidal predictions are a matter of safety and economic stability. Harbor operations, fishing schedules, and construction projects all depend on knowing exactly when the water level will change. Modern technology allows for precise forecasts, yet nature retains a certain unpredictability. Respecting the ocean's power remains the most important lesson for those who live alongside its endless, rhythmic breathing.

Saunders College of Business (or SCB) (formerly known as The E. Philip Saunders College of Business) is one of eleven colleges at Rochester Institute of Technology and is accredited by the Association to Advance Collegiate Schools of Business (AACSB). As of fall semester 2018, Saunders College of Business encompasses nearly 11% of RIT's enrollment, home to more than 2,000 undergraduate and graduate students enrolled in programs across RIT Global Campuses in Rochester, New York, Croatia, Dubai, and Kosovo. Saunders College works in partnership with RIT's entrepreneurial Venture Creations incubator and Albert J. Simone Center for Student Innovation and Entrepreneurship to integrate business education with RIT's technical and creative programs. Saunders College offers undergraduate (BS), Masters (MS), Masters of Business Administration (MBA), and Executive MBA (EMBA) programs.

The college dates back to 1910 with the establishment of the food administration and home economics departments at RIT. In 1952, RIT acquired the McKechnie-Lunger School of Commerce in Rochester, which was renamed after E. Philip Saunders in 2006. The college's dean is Jacqueline R. Mozrall. Hospitality and Tourism and Service Leadership programs were transitioned into the college from the College of Engineering Technology on July 1, 2019

Stress resultants are simplified representations of the stress state in structural elements such as beams, plates, or shells. The geometry of typical structural elements allows the internal stress state to be simplified because of the existence of a "thickness'" direction in which the size of the element is much smaller than in other directions. As a consequence the three traction components that vary from point to point in a cross-section can be replaced with a set of resultant forces and resultant moments. These are the stress resultants (also called membrane forces, shear forces, and bending moment) that may be used to determine the detailed stress state in the structural element. A three-dimensional problem can then be reduced to a one-dimensional problem (for beams) or a two-dimensional problem (for plates and shells). Stress resultants are defined as integrals of stress over the thickness of a structural element. The integrals are weighted by integer powers the thickness coordinate z (or x3). Stress resultants are so defined to represent the effect of stress as a membrane force N (zero power in z), bending moment M (power 1) on a beam or shell (structure). Stress resultants are necessary to eliminate the z dependency of the stress from the equations of the theory of plates and shells.

Jean Tague-Sutcliffe (1931-1996) was an information scientist known for her contributions to the field of informetrics. She developed models for information measurement and information retrieval using empirical methods and statistical data. She served as Dean of the Graduate School of Library and Information Science at the University of Western Ontario from 1984 to 1995.

Tague-Sutcliffe obtained a bachelor of library science degree from McGill University and a Ph.D. from Western Reserve University. Her research primarily focused on the development of mathematical models for retrieval of information, with an emphasis on bibliometrics. She helped developed statistical tests for experiments run by the Text Retrieval Conference (TREC) in the 1990s. She became the Dean of the Graduate School of Library and Information Science at the University of Western Ontario in 1984 and served in that position until 1995, the year before her death. She was a long-time member of the American Society for Information Science (now known as the Association for Information Science and Technology, serving as Director-at-Large and winning two awards from the organization for her publications.

"It's Not Just Me, It's Everybody" is a song by American singer, songwriter, and musician Weyes Blood, which serves as the lead single for her fifth studio album And in the Darkness, Hearts Aglow. The song was released on September 12, 2022, by Sub Pop. The song was written by Weyes Blood, Ben Babbitt and Jonathan Rado. It was included in the set list of her In Holy Flux Tour.

Weyes Blood refers to the song as a "Buddhist anthem, ensconced in the interconnectivity of all beings, and the fraying of our social fabric." Musically, the track features swells of orchestral strings and harp from Mary Lattimore. Rolling Stone's Angie Martoccio called it a "dreamy six-minute" song "which opens with [the singer's] voice floating across the piano." BrooklynVegan's Bill Pearis called the song "gorgeous". Pitchfork chose the song as the best new track of the week, with their writer Allison Hussey saying "Over a soft bed of piano and percussion, Natalie Mering makes a blunt observation about the human condition", highlighting the lyrics "We've all become strangers/Even to ourselves". Hussey notes that "As Mering repeats the title refrain", the said refrain acts as an "assertion that she's not the only one suffering [which] lingers alongside her own reminder that 'it's all a part of the same thing': Being good to one another won't fix the world as it is, but it can at least make each day a little more bearable."

"A Brand New Day", also known as "Everybody Rejoice", is a song from the 1974 Broadway musical The Wiz written by American R&B singer and songwriter Luther Vandross.

In the musical, the song is sung to celebrate after Dorothy has killed Evillene, the tyrannical Wicked Witch of the West. Dorothy, the Tin Man, the Cowardly Lion, and the Scarecrow sing the song with the newly freed Winkies, who were ruled and enslaved by Evillene.

In 1975, Stephanie Mills (as Dorothy) performed the song on the original cast album for The Wiz. In 1976, Vandross recorded a version of the song for his album Luther, on Cotillion Records.

It was later featured in the 1978 film version, sung by cast members Diana Ross, Michael Jackson, Nipsey Russell, and Ted Ross (credited as The Wiz Stars). Given the all-Black cast of The Wiz, the song's many references to freedom and new possibilities (especially as sung by African American characters who had just been freed from enslavement) certainly invoked the struggles and history of Blacks in America. In the onscreen version of the song, Nipsey Russell can even be heard exclaiming "Free at last!"-a reference to civil rights activist Martin Luther King Jr. (His impromptu addition to the song is not heard on the soundtrack album version, instead replaced by sung vocals by Ross.) The song's opening line is sung by Vandross, the song's composer (Vandross' line was to represent one of the Winkies singing and dancing on a table while throwing an item into the air). The film version was released as a single in some continental European countries and peaked at number one in Belgium and the Netherlands, credited to The Wiz Stars featuring Diana Ross and Michael Jackson.

The single release is an edit of the first half of the song, which in its entirety runs 7:49 on the film's soundtrack. It is backed by the second half of the song, which is labeled as "Liberation Ballet - A Brand New Day". The "Liberation Ballet" is primarily instrumental and is composed of uptempo dance music in a variety of styles, with the film's cast and choir cheering and singing "Can you feel the brand new day" throughout the piece.

"A Brand New Day", also known as "Everybody Rejoice", is a song from the 1974 Broadway musical The Wiz written by American R&B singer and songwriter Luther Vandross.
In the musical, the song is sung to celebrate after Dorothy has killed Evillene, the tyrannical Wicked Witch of the West. Dorothy, the Tin Man, the Cowardly Lion, and the Scarecrow sing the song with the newly freed Winkies, who were ruled and enslaved by Evillene.
In 1975, Stephanie Mills (as Dorothy) performed the song on the original cast album for The Wiz. In 1976, Vandross recorded a version of the song for his album Luther, on Cotillion Records.
It was later featured in the 1978 film version, sung by cast members Diana Ross, Michael Jackson, Nipsey Russell, and Ted Ross (credited as The Wiz Stars). Given the all-Black cast of The Wiz, the song's many references to freedom and new possibilities (especially as sung by African American characters who had just been freed from enslavement) certainly invoked the struggles and history of Blacks in America. In the onscreen version of the song, Nipsey Russell can even be heard exclaiming "Free at last!"-a reference to civil rights activist Martin Luther King Jr. (His impromptu addition to the song is not heard on the soundtrack album version, instead replaced by sung vocals by Ross.) The song's opening line is sung by Vandross, the song's composer (Vandross' line was to represent one of the Winkies singing and dancing on a table while throwing an item into the air). The film version was released as a single in some continental European countries and peaked at number one in Belgium and the Netherlands, credited to The Wiz Stars featuring Diana Ross and Michael Jackson.
The single release is an edit of the first half of the song, which in its entirety runs 7:49 on the film's soundtrack. It is backed by the second half of the song, which is labeled as "Liberation Ballet - A Brand New Day". The "Liberation Ballet" is primarily instrumental and is composed of uptempo dance music in a variety of styles, with the film's cast and choir cheering and singing "Can you feel the brand new day" throughout the piece.

Subject: Quick reminder on our team's data backup routine
Hi Team,
I wanted to take a moment to discuss the current state of our data backup habits. Over the past few months, I have noticed a gradual decline in consistency regarding the weekly offsite backups for our project files. While I understand that daily operational duties often take precedence and can lead to these tasks being pushed to the back of the mental queue, the risks associated with data loss are significant and cannot be overlooked. We are dealing with sensitive client information, proprietary code, and years of accumulated historical data that would be nearly impossible to reconstruct from scratch in the event of a hardware failure or accidental deletion. It is crucial that we view these backups not as an optional administrative chore, but as a fundamental security measure that protects both our reputation and our livelihood. I suspect that many of us simply forget to initiate the process because it is not an immediate part of our morning workflow, which is a common human error that we need to mitigate through better organization rather than relying on memory alone.
The current manual method we are using is prone to inconsistency because it depends entirely on an individual remembering to plug in the external drive and click the start button. This single point of failure is problematic. I have been looking into automating this process within our existing server environment so that the backup runs automatically every Sunday night at two in the morning. This timing ensures that the system is relatively idle, minimizing any performance impact on our daytime operations, and it eliminates the need for anyone to physically remember to perform the task. Automation also allows us to send a simple confirmation email to a shared management inbox upon successful completion. If that email does not arrive by Monday morning, it serves as an immediate alert that something went wrong, allowing us to address the issue before it becomes a catastrophe. This shift from manual to automated should significantly reduce the cognitive load on each of us and ensure that the backups happen with the same reliability as our other scheduled system maintenance tasks.
In addition to implementing the automated schedule, I would like to propose a quarterly audit of our backup integrity. It is not enough to simply assume that the files are backing up correctly; we need to periodically verify that the backups are actually restorable. I suggest we designate one person per quarter to perform a test restore of a small subset of random files to a temporary directory. We will then compare these restored files against the live versions to ensure there is no corruption during the transfer process. This verification step is often skipped in many organizations because it seems redundant, but it is the only way to have true confidence in our disaster recovery plan. By catching any potential issues early, such as file system errors or storage device degradation, we can prevent small problems from growing into critical failures. We can document the results of these quarterly tests in a simple log file that will also be backed up, creating a traceable history of our data management efforts over time.
I would appreciate it if everyone could review their personal local backups as well. While this new system covers our central server, many of us likely keep drafts or private notes on our local machines that are not part of the central repository. Please ensure that your personal documents are also being synced to a secure cloud location or a dedicated local drive that is separate from your main operating system partition. Data hygiene is a shared responsibility, and strengthening the overall security of our team starts with each individual taking ownership of their own digital footprint. I have attached a link to a brief guide on best practices for local encryption and secure cloud storage options if anyone needs a refresher on those specific topics. Let us aim to make these procedures a standard part of our professional toolkit rather than an exception that we only remember after something goes wrong.
I will set up the initial automation script by next Wednesday and send out the test confirmation emails so we can all confirm that the new workflow is working as intended. Please feel free to reach out if you have any questions, concerns, or suggestions for improving this process further. My goal is to make this as seamless and low-effort as possible for everyone, so that data security becomes a background feature of our work environment rather than a recurring source of stress. Thank you for your attention to this matter and for your continued commitment to maintaining a robust and secure digital workspace for the entire team.
Best regards,
Alex Mercer
IT Operations Manager

Ridgeview Trail Sector 4 is currently open to the public with moderate difficulty ratings. Recent rainfall has softened the dirt paths near the lower switchbacks, so hikers should expect sticky mud underfoot. The upper sections remain dry and stable, offering clear visibility due to recent clearing work by the maintenance crews. Flashy boots or waterproof footwear are strongly recommended for the first two miles before the terrain firms up near the ridgeline.

Flash flooding risks have decreased significantly since the previous advisory. Water levels at Creek Crossing are within normal limits, though the current remains stronger than average. Life vests are not required, but caution is advised for those using the designated stepping stones. Please monitor the river gauge at the trailhead kiosk before attempting the crossing during late morning hours when snowmelt typically peaks.

Wildlife sightings have increased near the meadow rest area. Bear activity persists, so maintain proper distance and secure all food storage. No damaged property or injuries have been reported in this sector over the last week. Rangers patrol the trail twice daily, ensuring safety protocols are followed and reporting any urgent hazards to the central dispatch office immediately.

Facilities at the main trailhead are fully operational. Restrooms are cleaned every four hours, and the parking lot has sufficient capacity for seasonal use. Free maps and first-aid kits are available at the information booth. Staff encourage visitors to check local weather forecasts before departure, as afternoon thunderstorms are possible during this time of year.

Leave No Trace principles must be observed strictly. Carry out all trash and pack in toilet paper if using primitive facilities. Off-trail hiking is prohibited to protect fragile alpine vegetation. Volunteering for cleanup efforts is welcome, and volunteers can sign up at the ranger station. Safe travels and enjoy the natural beauty responsibly.

To: All Events Coordination Staff 
From: Director of Venue Operations 
Date: October 8, 2026 
Subject: Updated Procedures for Wedding Venue Booking

Effective immediately, all wedding reservations must be processed through the central booking portal, and no manual entries will be accepted. The portal now requires the submission of a completed client questionnaire, a signed venue agreement, and a non-refundable deposit of 25 percent of the estimated total cost. Once these items are received, the system will generate a confirmation number that must be referenced in all subsequent communications. Failure to follow this workflow will result in the reservation being placed on hold until compliance is achieved, and may lead to loss of the preferred booking date.

Clients are required to schedule an on-site walkthrough within ten business days of their initial inquiry. The walkthrough must be conducted by a senior events planner who will verify the feasibility of the requested dates, assess any special accommodations, and confirm compliance with local noise ordinances and occupancy limits. After the walkthrough, a detailed event timeline should be drafted and emailed to the couple for approval. Any changes to the timeline after the final approval must be documented and signed off by both the client and the venue manager to avoid scheduling conflicts.

All catering arrangements must be coordinated with the approved list of in-house vendors, unless an external caterer receives prior written exemption from the culinary director. External vendors are required to submit proof of liability insurance and a copy of their food safety certification before they may be allowed on the premises. The venue's kitchen staff will be briefed on the menu at least three days before the event, and a final headcount must be provided no later than 48 hours prior to the wedding ceremony. Late changes to the menu or headcount may incur additional fees as outlined in the venue agreement.

Security and parking logistics are to be finalized during the final planning meeting, which should occur at least two weeks before the wedding date. The security coordinator will assign staff for crowd control, monitor entry points, and ensure that all emergency exits remain unobstructed. Parking allocations must accommodate the expected number of guests, and any overflow arrangements should be communicated to the client in writing. All staff assigned to the event must complete the mandatory safety briefing and wear appropriate identification badges throughout the duration of the wedding.

Finally, after each wedding, the events team must complete a post-event report within five business days. The report should include a summary of any incidents, a checklist of services rendered, and feedback gathered from the client. This information will be used to refine our booking procedures and improve client satisfaction. Copies of the report are to be filed electronically under the event's confirmation number and a hard copy retained in the venue's archives for a minimum of three years.

baby sleep routines

A consistent bedtime routine can feel like a miracle for both parents and newborns, turning chaotic evenings into a predictable sequence that signals it's time to wind down. When a baby learns that certain cues-such as a dimmed lamp, a gentle lullaby, and a warm bath-foretell sleep, the brain begins to associate those actions with rest, making the transition smoother.

The first step is to establish a regular sleep window that aligns with the baby's natural circadian rhythm. Most infants thrive on a schedule that includes a late afternoon nap followed by a quiet, dimly lit period before bedtime. By keeping the timing consistent day after day, the child's internal clock learns when to feel sleepy, reducing the number of nightly awakenings.

A calm environment plays a crucial role in reinforcing the routine. Soft, white noise can mask household sounds that might otherwise startle a baby awake, while a comfortably cool room temperature helps maintain steady sleep. Swaddling younger infants or using a sleep sack for older babies offers a sense of security without the hazards of loose blankets.

Feeding before the final bedtime can also be a helpful component, as a full stomach often translates to longer, more restful periods of sleep. However, it's important not to overfeed, which can cause discomfort. A brief, soothing feed followed by gentle rocking or a quiet story can bridge the gap between waking and the drowsy state needed for a smooth drop into slumber.

Patience and flexibility remain essential. While routines provide structure, babies grow rapidly, and their sleep needs evolve. Adjusting the timing, duration of naps, or even the sequence of soothing activities may be necessary as the child reaches new milestones. By staying attuned to these changes, parents can keep the routine effective and maintain the peace that a good night's sleep brings to the whole family.

Ride Out (album)

Ride Out is the seventeenth studio album by American rock singer-songwriter Bob Seger. The album was released on October 14, 2014. Although Seger had previously stated that it might be his final album, a follow-up album entitled I Knew You When, composed mainly of previously unreleased tracks, was released on November 17, 2017.

Ride Out was Seger's first album of new material in eight years. After 2006's Face the Promise, it was the second studio album since 1975 to be credited to Bob Seger rather than Bob Seger & The Silver Bullet Band.

Rumors about the album started to spread as far back as 2010. On July 13, 2011, Bob Seger reported via Facebook that he was recording new material at Ocean Way in Nashville. A Rolling Stone article from February 16, 2012 suggested that the album would be released in September of that year; however, the album did not come out. On April 11, 2013, Seger told the audience at a live performance in Detroit: "We should have our new album out in late August-if we are lucky." That date was also not met. The official announcement of the album was finally made on August 18, 2014. Seger stated that he really made an effort to "break new ground" on this album and, therefore, none of the songs on it would sound quite like anything he had done before. Seger said he approached this album differently in terms of feels and speeds.

The official announcement of the album was preceded by the release of the lead single "Detroit Made" to radio stations on August 14, 2014. The album title, artwork and release date were announced on August 18, 2014. The album was scheduled to be released by Capitol Records on October 14, 2014. Initially, no other information besides the release date was made public. On August 28, 2014, a photograph "showing a hand-written list of 13 truncated song titles on top of a studio mixing board" was posted on Seger's official Facebook page. Although this appeared to be the track listing of Ride Out, the final list of songs to be included in the album was not announced officially until September 9, 2014 when the album became available for pre-order on iTunes and Amazon.com. Besides the regular 10-track album, an expanded deluxe edition with three additional tracks and different artwork is available. Both editions were released on compact disc. Target offers an exclusive version of the deluxe edition with two additional bonus tracks. The album is available as a digital download as well, although the majority of Seger's back catalog was not yet available for purchase in digital format. Unlike Seger's past few albums since 1994's Greatest Hits, Ride Out is also available on vinyl in a 180-gram pressing aimed at audiophiles.

Alongside six of Seger's original compositions, the album includes a number of cover versions, which is not common for Seger as his albums usually contain no more than one or two songs that he did not write himself or in collaboration. One exception from that rule is the cover album Smokin' O.P.'s from 1972.

On Ride Out, Seger chose to include a total of four cover songs by well-known singer-songwriters of the country and Americana genres. Two of the songs are classics of the genre while the other two were released fairly recently.

The uptempo rock song "Detroit Made" was written by American singer-songwriter John Hiatt as "a musical mash note to the Buick Electra 225" It was first released by Hiatt himself on his 2011 album Dirty Jeans and Mudslide Hymns.

"The Devil's Right Hand" is an alternative country classic by Steve Earle from his 1988 album Copperhead Road. Versions of the song were recorded by country legends Johnny Cash and Waylon Jennings among others.

research grant timeline

Most researchers underestimate the sheer duration of the grant application cycle. From initial concept to final award notification, the process often stretches over twelve to eighteen months. This extended timeline requires meticulous planning, as every phase has strict internal and external deadlines that cannot be missed. Understanding this flow is essential for maintaining research continuity and ensuring funding secures the necessary resources before they are actually needed.

The preparatory phase begins well before any official submission date. Investigators must gather preliminary data, consult with program officers, and draft a robust proposal narrative. This stage typically takes three to four months, during which teams refine their scope, budget, and impact statements. Early engagement with potential co-investigators is crucial, as coordinating availability across multiple institutions adds significant logistical complexity to the schedule.

Official deadlines mark the next critical juncture. Submitting after the deadline usually means waiting another year for the same funding opportunity. Many agencies require internal pre-submission reviews, pushing the actual work start date even further back. Treating these internal milestones as absolute is vital, as the quality of the final document depends heavily on the feedback incorporated during these preliminary steps.

Following submission, the review process consumes several months. Peer review panels evaluate merit, significance, and approach, often leading to a waiting period that can feel endless for applicants. During this time, no changes can be made to the proposal, and investigators usually shift focus to other projects or administrative duties. The uncertainty of this period is a constant psychological burden, requiring resilience and forward-looking strategies.

Upon notification, the award process itself takes time. Administrative offices send offer letters, which require negotiation and acceptance before funds are released. Final contracts and terms and conditions must be signed by authorized institutional representatives. Only after these legalities are resolved can the team formally begin spendable activities, marking the true start of the funded research period.

1K ZX Chess

1K ZX Chess's code takes up only 672 bytes in memory, but implements chess rules except for castling, promotion, and en passant, including a computer opponent. It was the smallest implementation of chess on any computer at the time. Developer David Horne discussed 1K ZX Chess and published the full source code as a type-in program in a series of articles in Your Computer in 1982 and 1983.

Popular Computing Weekly in 1982 called 1K ZX Chess "one of the most interesting ZX tapes to pass through our office in recent weeks". It approved of the computer displaying moves while considering them and noted "the skills which went into writing a chess program in 1K of machine code. Is there anyone reading this who could even contemplate doing the same?" The magazine concluded, "Despite the limitations this is one cassette, at £3, which I would recommend." Sinclair User in 1983 stated that "it takes some technical wizardry to squeeze this kind of game into the unexpanded ZX81". The magazine praised the game's quick loading speed, and found that it "makes its moves very fast for the amount of memory available for it". Home Computing Weekly gave the game three out of five stars, criticizing the confusing user interface but stating that "it still produces play which needs some thought to beat". Tim Harding wrote in a 1985 book on computer chess that "the man who did it must be some sort of genius". While describing 1K ZX Chess' quality of play as "so appalling that it would be hard to make it beat you" and criticizing the backward algebraic notation, he concluded that "the program is nevertheless a fantastic technical achievement". A breakdown of all the optimizations was provided in a rebuild of the original source. 1K ZX Chess came in second place for best software in a poll of ZX81 users. Retrogaming Times Monthly described it as "history's greatest game programming feat"; Kuro5hin agreed, calling 1K ZX Chess "the greatest program ever written". BootChess author Olivier Poudade praised 1K ZX Chess's code, stating that at first writing a smaller chess program "seemed impossible ... Horne had nailed it so much already". Poudade acknowledged replicating some of Horne's methods as he could not improve them.

Photography is a craft that blends art and science, and the best way to start is by mastering a few fundamental concepts. At its core, a camera is a light-gathering device that captures an image on a sensor or film. Understanding how the three main exposure settings-aperture, shutter speed, and ISO-work together is essential for turning a scene into a well-balanced photograph. Aperture controls the size of the lens opening, influencing how much light reaches the sensor and how much of the scene appears in focus. A wide aperture (low f-number) lets in more light and produces a shallow depth of field, ideal for portrait work where you want the subject to stand out against a creamy background. Conversely, a narrow aperture (high f-number) extends the depth of field, keeping both near and far objects sharp, which is useful for landscape photography.

Shutter speed determines how long the sensor is exposed to light. A fast shutter freezes motion, letting you capture a hummingbird's wings or a splash of water without blur. A slow shutter, on the other hand, can convey movement through intentional blur, such as the smooth ribbons of light from passing cars at night. When using slower speeds, a tripod becomes a valuable tool to avoid unwanted camera shake, while handheld shooting often requires a higher ISO to compensate for reduced light. ISO measures the sensor's sensitivity to light; raising ISO makes the sensor more receptive, allowing you to shoot in dim conditions, but it can also introduce grain or noise, which may or may not be desirable depending on the aesthetic you're aiming for.

Composition is the next pillar of photography basics. The rule of thirds, though simple, offers a reliable framework for placing subjects off-center to create a more dynamic image. Imagine your viewfinder divided into nine equal sections by two vertical and two horizontal lines; positioning key elements along these lines or at their intersections tends to draw the eye naturally. Beyond this rule, look for leading lines, patterns, and contrast to guide the viewer's attention. A strong foreground element can add depth, while a clear focal point ensures the image has purpose. Pay attention to the edges of the frame; stray objects or distracting backgrounds can pull focus away from the main subject.

Lighting is often called the photographer's greatest ally, and learning to read light will dramatically improve your work. Soft, diffused light-such as that on an overcast day-produces gentle shadows and is flattering for portraits. Harsh, direct sunlight creates strong contrast and can emphasize texture, making it perfect for architectural or street photography. Golden hour, the period shortly after sunrise or before sunset, offers warm tones and elongated shadows that add mood and dimension. When natural light isn't available or you need more control, artificial sources like flashes or continuous LED lights can be used to shape illumination and fill shadows.

Finally, practice and experimentation are what turn knowledge into skill. Start by shooting in manual mode, even if it feels intimidating at first; this forces you to consider each exposure element deliberately. Review your images on a computer, zooming in to assess sharpness, exposure, and composition. Don't be afraid to make mistakes-overexposed frames, blurry shots, or odd color casts are all part of the learning curve. As you grow more comfortable, explore different genres, lenses, and post-processing techniques to develop your personal style. With patience and curiosity, the basics of photography become a launchpad for endless creative possibilities.
